sections.readable_text:
An archaeological site spans [MATH: 1.1\,\textrm{mi}^2.] What is the total area of the site in square yards?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]

sections.normalized_html:
We want to convert the area of the site from square miles to square yards.

We are told that there are [MATH: 1,760\,\textrm{yd}] per [MATH: \textrm{mi},] which we can write as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{1,760\,\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{mi}}]

We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get

[MATH: ((1, 760yd)/(mi))^{2}|= (1, 760^{2}yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}).]

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying [MATH: 1.1\,\textrm{mi}^2] by our conversion factor, we get

[MATH: 1.1mi^{2}|= 1.1mi^{2} ⋅ (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = 1.1mi^{2} ⋅ (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = 1.1 ⋅ 3, 097, 600yd^{2}; = 3, 407, 360yd^{2}.]

Therefore, the total area of the site is [MATH: 3,407,360\,\textrm{yd}^2.]

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]

sections.normalized_html:
We want to convert the area from square yards to square miles.

We are given that there are [MATH: 1,760] yards per mile, which we can write as follows: [MATH: \dfrac{1,760 \, \textrm{yd}}{\textrm{mi}}] We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get [MATH: ((1, 760yd)/(mi))^{2}|= (1, 760^{2}yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}).]

However, since we're converting from a smaller unit of area [MATH: (\textrm{yd})^2] to a larger one [MATH: (\textrm{mi})^2,] we need to multiply [MATH: 3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2] by the reciprocal of the above: [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mi}^2}{3,097,600 \, \textrm{yd}^2}] This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying [MATH: 3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2] by our conversion factor, we get [MATH: 3, 872, 000yd^{2}|= 3, 872, 000yd^{2} ⋅ (mi^{2})/(3, 097, 600yd^{2}); = 3, 872, 000yd^{2} ⋅ (mi^{2})/(3, 097, 600yd^{2}); = (3, 872, 000)/(3, 097, 600)mi^{2}; = 1.25mi^{2},] rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the area is approximately [MATH: 1.25\,\textrm{mi}^2.]

sections.normalized_html:
A maglev train accelerates at a rate of [MATH: 5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}.] What is this acceleration rate, in miles per minute squared, rounded to the nearest tenth?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,609\,\textrm{m}]
sections.readable_text:
A maglev train accelerates at a rate of [MATH: 5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}.] What is this acceleration rate, in miles per minute squared, rounded to the nearest tenth?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,609\,\textrm{m}]

sections.normalized_html:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{m}] to [MATH: \textrm{mi}.]

[MATH: \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{m}} }{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\cancel{\textrm{m}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{s}^2] into [MATH: \textrm{min}^2.]

[MATH: \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{m}} }{ \cancel{\textrm{s}^2} }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\cancel{\textrm{m}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \cancel{\textrm{s}^2} }{ \textrm{min}^2 } = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}]

So, our conversion formula is [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{ \textrm{s}^2 }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{m} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{s}^2 }{ \textrm{min}^2 } = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

  • The acceleration rate given in the problem statement is [MATH: 5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}.]

  • We are given that there are [MATH: 1,609] meters per mile. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1,609}] miles per meter.

  • There are [MATH: 60\,\textrm{s}] per [MATH: \textrm{min}.] We can write this as follows: [MATH: \dfrac{60\,\textrm{s}}{\textrm{min}}] To determine the number of seconds squared in one minute squared, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows: [MATH: ((60s)/(min))^{2}|= (60^{2}s^{2})/(min^{2}); = (3, 600s^{2})/(min^{2})]

Now, applying our conversion formula, we have [MATH: 5.6(m)/(s^{2})|= 5.6(m)/(s^{2}) ⋅ (1)/(1, 609)(mi)/(m) ⋅ 3, 600(s^{2})/(min^{2}); = (5.6 ⋅ (1)/(1, 609) ⋅ 3, 600)(m)/(s^{2}) ⋅ (mi)/(m) ⋅ (s^{2})/(min^{2}); = (5.6 ⋅ 3, 600)/(1, 609)(mi)/(min^{2}); = (20, 160)/(1, 609)(mi)/(min^{2}); ≈ 12.5(mi)/(min^{2}),] rounded to the nearest tenth.

Therefore, the maglev train is accelerating at a speed of approximately [MATH: 12.5\,\dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Questions about mixed units with squares are common on the math section of the SAT exam. In this topic, we'll practice these types of conversions.

---

Item 2 — Example: Converting Units of Area to Smaller Units

Example Prompt:
An archaeological site spans [MATH: 1.1\,\textrm{mi}^2.] What is the total area of the site in square yards?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We want to convert the area of the site from square miles to square yards.

We are told that there are [MATH: 1,760\,\textrm{yd}] per [MATH: \textrm{mi},] which we can write as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{1,760\,\textrm{yd}}{\textrm{mi}}]

We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get

[MATH: ((1, 760yd)/(mi))^{2}|= (1, 760^{2}yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}).]

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying [MATH: 1.1\,\textrm{mi}^2] by our conversion factor, we get

[MATH: 1.1mi^{2}|= 1.1mi^{2} ⋅ (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = 1.1mi^{2} ⋅ (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = 1.1 ⋅ 3, 097, 600yd^{2}; = 3, 407, 360yd^{2}.]

Therefore, the total area of the site is [MATH: 3,407,360\,\textrm{yd}^2.]

Item 5 — Example: Converting Units of Area to Larger Units

Example Prompt:
A professional sports complex covers [MATH: 3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2.] What is the area of the complex in square miles? Round your answer to two decimal places.

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,760\,\textrm{yd}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We want to convert the area from square yards to square miles.

We are given that there are [MATH: 1,760] yards per mile, which we can write as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{1,760 \, \textrm{yd}}{\textrm{mi}}]
We need to convert this into area units. So, by squaring this quantity and applying the rules of exponents, we get
[MATH: ((1, 760yd)/(mi))^{2}|= (1, 760^{2}yd^{2})/(mi^{2}); = (3, 097, 600yd^{2})/(mi^{2}).]

However, since we're converting from a smaller unit of area [MATH: (\textrm{yd})^2] to a larger one [MATH: (\textrm{mi})^2,] we need to multiply [MATH: 3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2] by the reciprocal of the above:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mi}^2}{3,097,600 \, \textrm{yd}^2}]
This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying [MATH: 3,872,000 \, \textrm{yd}^2] by our conversion factor, we get
[MATH: 3, 872, 000yd^{2}|= 3, 872, 000yd^{2} ⋅ (mi^{2})/(3, 097, 600yd^{2}); = 3, 872, 000yd^{2} ⋅ (mi^{2})/(3, 097, 600yd^{2}); = (3, 872, 000)/(3, 097, 600)mi^{2}; = 1.25mi^{2},]
rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the area is approximately [MATH: 1.25\,\textrm{mi}^2.]

Item 8 — Example: Converting Between Mixed Units Containing Squared Units of Time

Example Prompt:
A maglev train accelerates at a rate of [MATH: 5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}.] What is this acceleration rate, in miles per minute squared, rounded to the nearest tenth?

Hint: [MATH: 1\,\textrm{mi} = 1,609\,\textrm{m}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given the units [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2},] and we want to convert this into [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}.] We're converting two units instead of just one, so we're going to have to multiply by two conversion factors:

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}]

One of the conversion factors should change [MATH: \textrm{m}] to [MATH: \textrm{mi}.]

[MATH: \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{m}} }{\textrm{s}^2}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\cancel{\textrm{m}} } \cdot \,\dfrac{?}{?} = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}]

The other conversion factor should change [MATH: \textrm{s}^2] into [MATH: \textrm{min}^2.]

[MATH: \dfrac{\cancel{\textrm{m}} }{ \cancel{\textrm{s}^2} }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\cancel{\textrm{m}} } \cdot \dfrac{ \cancel{\textrm{s}^2} }{ \textrm{min}^2 } = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}]

So, our conversion formula is
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{m} }{ \textrm{s}^2 }\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{m} } \cdot \dfrac{ \textrm{s}^2 }{ \textrm{min}^2 } = \dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}.]

Now that we have our conversion formula, we need to determine the correct numbers to use and apply them.

- The acceleration rate given in the problem statement is [MATH: 5.6 \, \dfrac{\textrm{m}}{\textrm{s}^2}.]
- We are given that there are [MATH: 1,609] meters per mile. Taking the reciprocal, we find that there are [MATH: \dfrac{1}{1,609}] miles per meter.
- There are [MATH: 60\,\textrm{s}] per [MATH: \textrm{min}.] We can write this as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac{60\,\textrm{s}}{\textrm{min}}]
To determine the number of seconds squared in one minute squared, we square this quantity and apply the rules of exponents, as follows:
[MATH: ((60s)/(min))^{2}|= (60^{2}s^{2})/(min^{2}); = (3, 600s^{2})/(min^{2})]

Now, applying our conversion formula, we have
[MATH: 5.6(m)/(s^{2})|= 5.6(m)/(s^{2}) ⋅ (1)/(1, 609)(mi)/(m) ⋅ 3, 600(s^{2})/(min^{2}); = (5.6 ⋅ (1)/(1, 609) ⋅ 3, 600)(m)/(s^{2}) ⋅ (mi)/(m) ⋅ (s^{2})/(min^{2}); = (5.6 ⋅ 3, 600)/(1, 609)(mi)/(min^{2}); = (20, 160)/(1, 609)(mi)/(min^{2}); ≈ 12.5(mi)/(min^{2}),]
rounded to the nearest tenth.

Therefore, the maglev train is accelerating at a speed of approximately [MATH: 12.5\,\dfrac{\textrm{mi}}{\textrm{min}^2}.]
